225.hook: not by birth is one a brahmana, but by conduct; cut the stream, be bold

segments.voice: Every society has words of honor that come with a family name. Old money. Good family. A title you inherit. And most of us have met someone with every advantage of birth who behaved badly, and someone with none of them who was simply noble. The last chapter of the Dhammapada takes one of the most honored words of its world and asks a sharp question: what actually earns it? The chapter is forty-one verses long, the longest in the book, and nearly every verse ends the same way. Today: not by birth.

segments.voice: Today's word is brahmana, in Sanskrit brahmin. In the Buddha's India, brahmins were the hereditary priestly class, the keepers of the Vedas and the sacred rites, and many were honored teachers; brahmins came to the Buddha as questioners, and many became his students. The Buddha didn't throw the word away. He kept it as a word of honor, and changed what it takes to earn it. In a sutta called the discourse on the outcast, he puts it directly: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. By deeds one becomes an outcast, and by deeds one becomes a brahmin. The Dhammapada's last chapter is built on that idea. It opens with courage: cut off the stream of craving, be bold, drive away desire. When you understand how things come to an end, it says, you know the unmade. Then a lovely verse about light. The sun shines by day, the moon by night, the warrior shines in armor, the brahmana in meditation; but the Buddha shines day and night. And a verse full of wordplay. One is called a brahmana because he has put evil away, a samana, a renunciant, because he lives in calm, and a pabbajita, one gone forth, because he has sent his own impurities away. The chapter's refrain, which runs through all four days of this chapter, is: him I call a brahmana. Each verse fills it with conduct: patience, gentleness, truth, freedom from clinging. Nobility, in this chapter, is something you do.

segments.voice: We all wear badges. Some are literal: a uniform, a lanyard, a ring. Some are subtler: the right sneakers, the reading list on the coffee table, the practice you mention casually at dinner. Spiritual life has its badges too. A string of beads on the wrist, the right vocabulary, a meditation app streak you'd rather people noticed. In the Buddha's India, the badge of a holy man was often his hair, grown long and matted, and a robe of animal skin. Today's verses look straight at the badge. Today: not by matted hair.
screen: `WE ALL WEAR BADGES.` → `SPIRITUAL LIFE HAS THEM TOO.` → `LONG, MATTED HAIR.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred ninety-three, in Max Müller's English: "A man does not become a Brahmana by his plaited hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana." Plaited, or matted, hair was the sign of a certain kind of ascetic in ancient India, many of them devoted, serious people. The verse isn't mocking them. It's saying the sign isn't the thing. The next verse says it more sharply, speaking straight to someone vain about his look: what use is your matted hair, what use your robe of goatskin? The inside is a tangle, and you're polishing the outside. Then the verses turn to the real thing, and the picture is surprising. The one this chapter honors might wear rags taken from a rubbish heap, be thin enough that you can see the veins, and sit alone in the forest, meditating. No badge at all. One verse even plays with how people addressed each other. Someone with plenty of possessions, the text says, might be called sir, but he isn't a brahmana for that. The brahmana is the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing. Then the portrait keeps filling in. The one who has cut every fetter and trembles at nothing. The one who bears insults, blows and even chains without anger, whose patience is an army. The one free of anger, faithful in duty, keeping the precepts, tamed. This is the fourth time in these weeks that the book has said it: the robe, the shaved head, the gray hair and now the matted hair aren't the point. The heart is.

227.title: Water on a lotus leaf (401–410)
227.hook: like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on a needle's point, pleasures don't cling
227.howItsDone: The lotus is one of the most common symbols in Buddhist art, often shown beneath the Buddha's seat; teachers use the water-on-a-lotus-leaf image for living in the world without clinging to it.

segments.voice: If you've ever seen rain fall on a lotus pond, you've seen something a little magical. The drops land on the broad green leaves and don't soak in. They bead up into bright little balls, roll around, and slide off, leaving the leaf completely dry. Scientists have a name for it now, the lotus effect, and they've studied the leaf's tiny waxy bumps to make self-cleaning surfaces. Buddhists noticed it much earlier, and saw in it a picture of a free mind. Today: water on a lotus leaf.
screen: `RAIN ON A LOTUS POND.` → `THE DROPS BEAD UP AND ROLL OFF.` → `THE LEAF STAYS DRY.`

segments.voice: Verse four hundred one, in Max Müller's English: "Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle." Two pictures. The water rolls off the leaf. And a mustard seed, tiny and round, can't balance on a needle's point; it just drops. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the rain never falls, or that pleasure never touches this person. The lotus lives in the pond. The rain lands. Pleasant things arrive, and are enjoyed, and they don't soak in and take hold. A few verses later, the mustard seed comes back: greed, hatred, pride and envy have dropped away from this person like a mustard seed from a needle's point. Then the chapter's portrait keeps growing, verse by verse. The one who has put down the burden. The one of deep wisdom who knows the right road from the wrong. The one who has laid down the rod toward every living being, weak or strong, and neither kills nor causes killing. Gentle among the violent, calm among the grasping. The one whose speech is true, useful and never harsh. The one who takes nothing that isn't given, long or short, large or small, good or bad. This is the third brahmana day, and you can hear the book gathering everything it has taught: harmlessness, patience, true speech, not taking, not clinging. And the lotus, which appeared back in chapter four growing from a rubbish heap, returns here as the picture of the whole thing: in the water, not soaked by it.

228.title: The end of the path (411–423)
228.hook: the one gone beyond both good and evil ties, bright as the moon, who has reached the end
228.howItsDone: In Theravada tradition the brahmana chapter is read as a portrait of the arahant, one who has reached the end of the path; monks often chant the Dhammapada in full at special occasions, and many lay Buddhists read it through more than once.

segments.voice: There's a particular feeling when you reach the last page of a long book. You slow down. You read the final lines twice. Part of you wants it to go on, and part of you is proud you're here at all. Seventy-one days ago, we opened the Dhammapada, and its first verse said: the mind comes first. Today we read its last thirteen verses, four hundred eleven to four hundred twenty-three, and close the book. It ends, fittingly, with a portrait of someone who has arrived. Today: the end of the path.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A LONG BOOK.` → `SEVENTY-ONE DAYS AGO: THE MIND FIRST.` → `A PORTRAIT OF ARRIVAL.`

segments.voice: The last verses finish the portrait of the brahmana, the one who has reached the end. He has no longings left, and no doubts; he has touched the deathless. Then a surprising line: this one has gone beyond both good and evil, beyond the ties of both. It doesn't mean he stopped caring about goodness. The tradition reads it as going beyond the pull of both kinds of karma, good and bad, the fuel that keeps the wheel of rebirth turning. He is free of grief and stain, the verse says, and the next compares him to the moon: bright, clear, serene, undisturbed. Then pictures you'll recognize from our weeks together. He has crossed the muddy, difficult road of rebirth, and reached the far shore. His path can't be traced, the text says, not by gods or spirits or people, like the birds in the sky from chapter seven. He calls nothing his own, before, behind or in between, the words the acrobat Uggasena heard on his pole. And the last verse, four hundred twenty-three, describes the one who remembers his former lives, sees the heavens and the lower states, and has reached the end of births: a sage, complete. That's where the book stops. Not with a rule, or a command, but with a picture of freedom. The Dhammapada began with a choice, the mind coming first, and pain following a bad thought like a wheel following an ox. It ends with the wheel standing still. Whether you read it as a promise, a portrait or a direction to walk, you have now read the whole thing, twenty-six chapters, four hundred twenty-three verses.

segments.voice: Think about the songs you know by heart. You never sat down to memorize most of them. They just stuck, because at some point they meant something to you, and now they come back at odd moments: in the shower, in the car, on a hard day. A book of verses works the same way. You've read four hundred twenty-three of them. Most will blur. But a handful have probably already stuck, and those are the ones that will come back when you need them. Today we go looking for them. segments.voice: The Dhammapada was made to be carried this way. For centuries, most people who knew it didn't own a copy. They knew verses: a few learned as children, a few heard in a teacher's talk, a few chanted at a festival. Monks might learn the whole book by heart; a grandmother might know six verses and live by them. Both count. So here's a way to find yours. First, walk back through the book in your mind, chapter by chapter. The twin verses: the mind comes first. And verse five, in Max Müller's English: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Earnestness, and the island no flood can overwhelm. The fletcher straightening the arrow. The bee that takes nectar and leaves the flower. The spoon that never tastes the soup. The deep, still lake. Conquering yourself, rather than a thousand others. Drop by drop, the water pot fills. The world seen as a bubble. Not to do evil, to do good, to purify the mind: the teaching of all the Buddhas. Overcoming anger by not-anger. The Buddhas only point the way. The forest, the elephant, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Second, notice which ones tug at you. Not the ones you think you ought to pick, the ones that actually came back to you on some ordinary day. Third, write them down, in your own words if you like. There's no right list. Two people who read the same book will choose different verses, because they're living different lives. That's the point. A verse becomes yours when it has a job in your life.

230.title: The Dhammapada in the world
230.hook: carried across Asia in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit and Chinese; Max Müller brought it into English in 1870
230.howItsDone: The Pali Dhammapada is chanted and studied throughout Theravada Buddhism; related collections were kept by other early schools, and Tibetan and East Asian Buddhists know the sayings through the Udanavarga and Chinese versions.

segments.voice: In the eighteen nineties, in the desert near Khotan, on the old Silk Road in what is now western China, a French expedition came away with pieces of a very old manuscript. It was written on birch bark, in a script almost nobody could read anymore, in a language of the old northwest of India. When scholars finally worked it out, they found verses they knew. Here, thousands of miles from where the Pali canon was kept, someone had carried the same sayings you've been reading. Today: the Dhammapada in the world.
screen: `BIRCH BARK NEAR KHOTAN.` → `A SCRIPT ALMOST NO ONE COULD READ.` → `VERSES THEY KNEW.`

segments.voice: The version we've read is the Pali Dhammapada, kept by the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. But it has cousins. That birch-bark manuscript is called the Gandhari Dharmapada, after Gandhara, the region of today's northern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan where its language was spoken. Another version survives in a mixed Indian language and is named after the city of Patna. A larger Sanskrit collection called the Udanavarga, used by other early schools, shares hundreds of verses with it and was later translated into Tibetan. And the sayings went into Chinese early, in the third century, where they were read for centuries in monasteries. The collections don't match exactly. Chapters are arranged differently, some verses are missing, some are added. What's striking is how much stays the same across languages and centuries: hatred ending by not-hatred, the mind coming first, the bee and the flower. Then the verses traveled west. A Danish scholar, Viggo Fausböll, published the Pali text in Europe with a Latin translation in the eighteen fifties. Max Müller brought it into English in eighteen seventy and revised it in eighteen eighty-one for his great series, the Sacred Books of the East, the version we've read. Since then there have been dozens of English translations and many in other languages, and the book is still read by Buddhists and by people of other paths. Each of those carried it: monks memorizing on foot, scribes on birch bark, translators at desks. And now you, if you pass one verse along.

231.title: Camp 4 close: you read it
231.hook: 26 chapters, 423 verses: one whole book of the Buddha's sayings
231.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, reading or chanting the whole Dhammapada is a respected practice, and monastic students often memorize it; many lay Buddhists return to it through their lives, reading a verse or a chapter at a time.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dhammapada in the world, and your line: who else carried it. Did you pass a verse along to someone? Day two hundred thirty-one, the end of the week, and the last day of camp four.
screen: `THE DHAMMAPADA IN THE WORLD — WHO ELSE CARRIED IT.`

segments.voice: Plenty of people own a copy of the Dhammapada. It sits on shelves next to other books people mean to read someday. Plenty more have seen a verse from it on a poster, or a verse that was never in it at all. Very few sit down and read the whole thing, in order, from the first verse to the last. Seventy-four days ago, camp four began with a promise: all twenty-six chapters, all four hundred twenty-three verses, a few a day. You kept it. Today: you read it.
screen: `A COPY ON THE SHELF.` → `A VERSE ON A POSTER.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Let's gather the camp's words. Dhammapada: the path of the dhamma, and pada, a step and a line of verse. Appamada: earnestness, heedfulness, the path to the deathless. Citta: the mind, trembling like a fish on dry land, straightened like an arrow. Pandita: the wise one, who points out your faults like buried treasure. Arahant: the one whose path, like a bird's in the sky, can't be traced. Tanha: thirst, the creeper that grows while no one watches. Bhikkhu: the monk who lives on what is given, restrained in every sense. And brahmana: a title earned not by birth, but by conduct. Around those words, twenty-six chapters of pictures: the wheel following the ox, the island no flood can overwhelm, the spoon and the soup, the deep lake, the broken gong, the yellow leaf, the forest, the elephant, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. That's a whole book. Not a summary, not a quote on a mug: the book itself, in its own order. And now it ends where it began. Verse one, in Max Müller's English: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Hear it now, after four hundred twenty-two more verses, and it sounds different. You know what the book means by thought now: the mind that can be guarded, trained, emptied, and set free. Tomorrow, camp five begins: the depths. It opens with four rooms the Buddha said a person can live in: kindness, compassion, joy for others, and equanimity. Then the foundations of mindfulness, the Heart Sutra, the koans, and more.
screen: `EIGHT WORDS, DHAMMAPADA TO BRAHMANA.` · `TWENTY-SIX CHAPTERS OF PICTURES.` · `THE BOOK ITSELF, IN ITS OWN ORDER.` · `VERSE ONE, HEARD AGAIN.` · then, large: `YOU ACTUALLY READ IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. About ten weeks ago you met verse one. Let it come back now, slowly, one phrase per breath. All that we are. Breathe. Is the result of what we have thought. Breathe. Founded on our thoughts. Breathe. Made up of our thoughts. Then let the words go, and watch the thoughts themselves for a while, arriving and leaving, the raw material the whole book was about. No need to change them. Just see them. The bell holds the time.
Camp four close. Twenty-six chapters, four hundred twenty-three verses: one whole book of the Buddha's sayings, read in order.
screen: `CAMP 4 CLOSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you actually read it. Today, read verse one again, out loud or on paper, and notice how it sounds now. Day two hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 231 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOUR ROOMS TO LIVE IN.`
